options.text: In August 2014 you can stand where the water used to be, on the eastern lobe of the southern Aral Sea, and there is nothing under your boots but pale, cracked plates of clay running out to the horizon. According to NASA's Earth Observatory, that basin went completely dry that month. Fifty-four years earlier, in 1960, this was part of the fourth-largest lake on Earth. The towns on this shoreline fished it.

Here's a fact that sounds wrong: a sea can lose its water and get saltier at the same time. According to figures compiled in an environmental impact study of the Aral Sea crisis, salinity in the basin went from around 10 grams per litre to often more than 100, because the salt stayed and the water left. Evaporation beat the rivers. The Aral drew a fifth of its water from rain, and the rest from two rivers that were diverted.

The clue was in the pictures. Satellite images of the Aral Sea, the kind NASA's Earth Observatory publishes, show a coastline retreating from itself year after year, the same outline left stranded on dry land by maps drawn a generation earlier. According to an environmental impact study of the Aral Sea crisis, after fifty years the lake's area was a quarter of its original size, holding a tenth of its water. Something upstream was taking it.

Start with the distance. The water in the Aral Sea came from snowmelt in distant mountains, carried across the desert by the Syr Darya and the Amu Darya. According to an environmental impact study of the Aral Sea crisis, a quarter to three-quarters of the water going through the Soviet canals, depending on the period, was absorbed into the sand and wasted. A river system poured into a desert. Fifty-four years later, the eastern basin was dust.

Here's what isn't settled. According to an environmental impact study of the Aral Sea crisis, the southern part of the sea has been unable to be restored to its former state, and the report's authors say a greater solution still needs to be found. They argue for planting Saxaul across the dry bed; others propose drip irrigation, boycotting Uzbek cotton, or redirecting the Ob River south. Which one works? Nobody has settled it.

why: It puts a half-watching viewer on the cracked seabed in the exact month NASA's Earth Observatory says the basin went dry, and every figure in it comes straight from the dossier.
